survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD country note summarises indicators from Education at a Glance 2025 using the latest available reference years, but it does not provide microdata or an analysis section describing student-level sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. The document reports descriptive system-level statistics (e.g., attainment shares, unemployment rates by education level, expenditure per student, teacher staffing indicators) rather than estimating model-based effects from a student sample. As a result, there is no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) to specify for replication within this note. For users who access the underlying OECD indicator datasets, weighting and variance estimation should follow the methodological documentation referenced by the note (Education at a Glance 2025: Sources, Methodologies and Technical Notes; OECD Handbook for Internationally Comparative Education Statistics 2018).

data.outcome_summary: Education at a Glance 2025: Portugal (EN) is a descriptive OECD country note that summarises key characteristics of Portugal’s education system using the latest available indicator data. It highlights tertiary attainment trends (e.g., 25–34 year-olds with tertiary education rising from 38% to 43% between 2019 and 2024), educational inequality by parental education (a large tertiary-attainment gap among 25–34 year-olds), and labour-market associations with education (notably higher earnings and lower unemployment for tertiary-educated adults). The note also reports system inputs and constraints, including expenditure per student relative to GDP per capita, teacher staffing pressures (instruction hindered by lack of teaching staff, rising share of non-fully qualified teachers), and instructional time and class size patterns. Because the note does not conduct student-level predictive modeling, it does not report ML performance metrics, plausible-value estimation, or missing-data procedures; policy interpretation should therefore focus on the reported indicator patterns rather than causal claims.
